title: Prompting for Coding Agents
description: Write prompts that provide intent, scope, context, constraints, evidence, and verification without micromanaging every token.

lessons.title: State the objective first
lessons.principle: Agents perform better when the desired outcome is unambiguous.
lessons.practice: Open with the user-visible or engineering result, not a long chronology.

lessons.title: Give relevant context
lessons.principle: A model cannot infer private repository conventions it has not seen.
lessons.practice: Point to files, modules, architecture notes, examples, and existing patterns that matter.

lessons.title: Name hard constraints
lessons.principle: Constraints reduce plausible but unacceptable solutions.
lessons.practice: Specify compatibility, libraries, security rules, performance budgets, and forbidden changes.

lessons.title: Define scope explicitly
lessons.principle: Agents may broaden tasks to adjacent cleanup.
lessons.practice: List the files or subsystems in scope and call out unrelated refactors as out of scope.

lessons.title: Provide acceptance criteria
lessons.principle: The agent needs a concrete target for deciding whether work is complete.
lessons.practice: Include testable outcomes and failure cases in the initial prompt.

lessons.title: Ask for inspection before editing
lessons.principle: Immediate edits can encode a wrong mental model of the codebase.
lessons.practice: Require the agent to inspect relevant implementation, tests, and configuration before changing behavior.

lessons.title: Request a plan for complex work
lessons.principle: Planning exposes misunderstandings before they become large diffs.
lessons.practice: For multi-file or risky tasks, ask for a brief plan tied to requirements and validation.

lessons.title: Use examples strategically
lessons.principle: Examples communicate format and edge behavior efficiently.
lessons.practice: Provide one or two representative examples without overfitting the solution to a single case.

lessons.title: Include known failure evidence
lessons.principle: Logs and reproducible symptoms are more useful than vague descriptions.
lessons.practice: Paste exact errors, failing inputs, screenshots, or steps to reproduce where possible.

lessons.title: Ask for assumptions
lessons.principle: Unstated assumptions are a major source of AI implementation drift.
lessons.practice: Have the agent list material assumptions and verify them against the repository or requirements.

lessons.title: Ask for minimal changes
lessons.principle: Minimality reduces regression surface and review cost.
lessons.practice: Tell the agent to prefer the smallest coherent implementation that satisfies the spec.

lessons.title: Require existing patterns first
lessons.principle: New abstractions are often unnecessary when the codebase already has a convention.
lessons.practice: Ask the agent to reuse established components, services, utilities, and test patterns when suitable.

lessons.title: Use role instructions sparingly
lessons.principle: A role label is weaker than concrete constraints and evidence.
lessons.practice: Prefer precise engineering requirements over elaborate personas.

lessons.title: Avoid contradictory prompts
lessons.principle: Conflicting goals force the model to guess priorities.
lessons.practice: Order priorities and explicitly state which constraint wins when tradeoffs occur.

lessons.title: Ask for verification commands
lessons.principle: Agents should know how correctness will be demonstrated.
lessons.practice: Provide or request exact test, lint, typecheck, build, and focused validation commands.

lessons.title: Ask for a diff summary
lessons.principle: A concise behavioral summary helps review generated work.
lessons.practice: Require the agent to explain changed behavior, important design decisions, and residual risks.

lessons.title: Use follow-up prompts with evidence
lessons.principle: Feedback should close the loop on actual observed behavior.
lessons.practice: Report the failing assertion or undesired output and ask for root-cause correction rather than a random retry.

lessons.title: Separate investigation and implementation
lessons.principle: Premature editing can contaminate diagnosis.
lessons.practice: For unclear defects, explicitly request investigation only, then implement after the cause is established.

lessons.title: Constrain generated artifacts
lessons.principle: Generated schemas, migrations, configs, and documentation can have broad consequences.
lessons.practice: Specify exact formats, destinations, naming rules, and compatibility constraints.

lessons.title: Write prompts as executable briefs
lessons.principle: The strongest prompts resemble compact engineering tickets.
lessons.practice: Include objective, context, constraints, acceptance criteria, validation, and non-goals in a predictable structure.

codeExamples.snippet:
Objective: Fix duplicate form submissions.
Context: src/forms/submit.ts and its tests.
Constraints: no API contract changes.
Acceptance: one server write per user action.
Validate: npm test -- submit

Investigate only.
1. Reproduce the failure.
2. Identify the first violated invariant.
3. Cite the relevant code path.
4. Do not edit files yet.
